title: All or Nothing Means I’m Always Right
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Binary thinking is examined here as a cognitive defect with organisational consequences. The author concedes the appeal up front: collapsing the gray is cognitively efficient, saves time, and supplies conviction while relieving the obligation to stay open to competing views, and everyone does it occasionally. The question the piece pursues is what happens when absolutes become a leader's default. The answer is that data gets pushed to fit the extremes — people become good or bad, trustworthy or deceitful, tasks pass or fail, outcomes are victory or defeat — and a world without contradiction or unresolved tension makes decisions feel easier than they are, culminating in the belief that one is always right. The causal account is the counterintuitive part: the habit is generated by an intolerance for indecision, so complexity produces either forced simplification or an abrupt surrender. The remedies are structural rather than therapeutic — put such leaders on teams that must work a problem through, slow the decision process down, and withhold unilateral authority by requiring consensus, or remove positional power altogether. The final warning is about propagation: their decisions are usually flawed and the people they reward sound just like them.
points: The author identifies the payoff that sustains the habit — conviction plus cognitive efficiency — which explains why argument alone does not dislodge it.
The causal claim is that absolutism grows out of an inability to tolerate indecision, so the same leaders who force binaries also abandon problems quickly when nuance is unavoidable.
The remedies are procedural, not persuasive: deliberate group processes that slow decisions down are what put a dent in the worldview.
The governance recommendation is concrete — require consensus before conclusions, withhold unilateral decision rights, and failing that remove the positional power to lead.
The closing observation that such leaders reward people who sound just like them makes the defect self-replicating through hiring and promotion.
quotes: Feeling strongly about an issue or person encourages even the best leaders on occasion to eliminate the gray and to see things in black and white.
Landing firmly and rigidly on a preferred square is both cognitively efficient and saves time.
When a leader begins to see everything as all or nothing, they push information and data to fit the extremes.
Because they see a world without contradiction, competing goals, and unresolved tensions, they soon begin to think decisions are easier than they are.
Ironically, it is the need to overcome indecision that typically produces this abnormality in thinking.
Organizations would do best not to give leaders with this flaw the power to make unilateral decisions.
It is smart to remember the decisions they make are usually flawed and the people they reward sound just like them.
